questions.question: After Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness, the tempter challenges him to turn stones into bread, jump from the temple pinnacle, and bow for global political power. What common thread defines how Jesus shuts down all three offers?
options: He refuses to use his authority for personal relief, public spectacle, or shortcuts around suffering
He debates the tempter by proving that physical hunger and earthly kingdoms are illusions
He summons angels immediately after the first challenge to end the confrontation by force
He agrees to perform the signs later in Jerusalem once his disciples are gathered to witness them
questions.explanation: Each temptation offers a real-world shortcut—instant physical relief, viral spectacle to force belief, or raw political leverage—and Jesus rejects all three by anchoring to foundational covenant boundaries.

questions.question: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus addresses people who pride themselves on never committing murder. Where does he relocate the actual moral boundary?
options: To the government courts that fail to prosecute violent offenders swiftly
To the internal contempt, nursing of anger, and verbal character assassination that precede violence
To the temple priests who accept sacrifices without interviewing the worshipers first
To the Roman soldiers who enforce public order through intimidation
questions.explanation: Jesus strips away the comfort of mere technical compliance with the law, pointing out that harboring contempt and dehumanizing someone verbally comes from the exact same root as physical violence.

questions.question: When Jesus critiques people who give charity and pray on busy street corners in Matthew 6, what does he say they have already received in full?
options: Forgiveness for their past financial dishonesty
Exemptions from the local synagogue tax
The public applause and social status they were actually chasing
A guaranteed leadership seat in the local council
questions.explanation: In Matthew 6:2-5, Jesus exposes performative virtue as a transaction for social clout: if you do good deeds to be seen by an audience, the audience's applause is the entire payout you will ever get.

questions.question: Jesus uses the image of someone obsessing over a tiny speck of sawdust in a friend's eye while ignoring a heavy timber plank in their own. What psychological blind spot is he diagnosing?
options: The inability to forgive people who have caused financial harm
The habit of avoiding confrontation when a friend is making a dangerous mistake
The tendency to use hyper-criticism of others' minor flaws to avoid confronting one's own massive failures
The fear of speaking publicly about moral standards in a hostile culture
questions.explanation: Notice Jesus does not say never help a friend remove the speck—he says extract your own plank first, because projection and self-righteousness ruin your vision to help anyone clearly.

questions.question: In Jesus' parable of the wheat and the weeds, why does the landowner forbid his field hands from ripping out the toxic weeds as soon as they spot them?
options: Because the weeds will naturally turn into wheat if given enough water and sunlight
Because aggressive, premature purges end up tearing out the healthy roots alongside the bad
Because the field hands were secretly the ones who planted the weeds at night
Because local agricultural law forbade harvesting anything before the autumn festival
questions.explanation: In Matthew 13:29, the owner recognizes that zealots trying to purify a mixed community too early lack the discernment to separate intertwined roots without destroying the good crop in the process.

questions.question: Moments after Peter is praised as 'the rock' for recognizing who Jesus is, what causes Jesus to turn around and call Peter a stumbling block?
options: Peter demands to be paid a salary as the head of the twelve disciples
Peter pulls Jesus aside to scold him for saying his mission requires suffering and execution
Peter refuses to share food with the Gentile crowds across the border
Peter falls asleep while standing guard outside the camp at Caesarea Philippi
questions.explanation: Peter wants a Messiah who wins through dominance, not sacrifice; when he tries to protect Jesus from the cross, Jesus exposes it as setting his mind on human ambition rather than God's purpose.

questions.question: A royal official has an astronomical, unpayable debt completely wiped clean by his king. What does that official do the moment he walks out of the palace?
options: He liquidates his remaining estate and distributes it to the poor
He grabs a peer by the throat over a trivial sum and throws him into debtor's prison
He flees the country before the king can reconsider the pardon
He falsifies the royal ledger to take credit for paying the debt himself
questions.explanation: Matthew 18:28-30 captures a brutal human hypocrisy: people who gladly accept massive grace for their own failures often enforce ruthless, zero-tolerance accounting on everyone underneath them.

questions.question: In the parable of the vineyard workers, the laborers hired at dawn receive the exact full day's wage they agreed to. Why do they turn furious at the end of the day?
options: The landowner deducts the cost of their tools from their final payout
The landowner pays the exact same full day's wage to workers who only clocked in for the final hour
The foreman delays their payment until the following week
The landowner forces them to harvest an extra field after sunset without overtime
questions.explanation: They weren't cheated out of a single coin, but watching latecomers receive equal generosity triggered status envy—proving how quickly comparison turns gratitude into resentment.

questions.question: In the parable of the talents, three servants are entrusted with capital while their master travels. Why is the third servant condemned when the master returns?
options: He embezzled the funds to buy personal land and lied about the accounting
He invested the money in a high-risk venture that went bankrupt during a famine
He buried the money in the dirt out of fear-driven paralysis and blamed the master's harshness
He gave the entire sum away to strangers without getting a receipt
questions.explanation: Notice the third servant didn't steal the money—he simply froze out of fear of failure, hid behind a cynical view of his master, and treated inaction as safety.

questions.question: At the Last Supper, Peter swears that even if every other disciple abandons Jesus, he will die before backing down. What actually breaks Peter's resolve a few hours later?
options: A Roman centurion holds a sword to his throat inside the governor's palace
The high priest offers him immunity if he testifies against Jesus in court
Casual questions from servant girls and bystanders around a courtyard fire
A written order from Pilate threatening to confiscate his fishing boats in Galilee
questions.explanation: Overconfident bravado in a safe room rarely survives sudden social pressure; Peter didn't fold under torture in a dungeon—he folded under the awkward gaze of servants by a fire.

questions.question: When four friends dig through a house roof to lower a paralyzed man in front of Jesus, why does Jesus first tell the man his sins are forgiven before healing his legs?
options: Because he did not realize the man was physically paralyzed until the crowd pointed it out
To force the critics in the room to confront that his visible healing proves his invisible authority to forgive
Because local Capernaum custom required a verbal blessing before touching a sick person
To delay the crowd while his disciples cleared an exit path through the doorway
questions.explanation: Anyone can claim an unverifiable inner credential ('your sins are forgiven'), so Jesus links the invisible claim to an undeniable physical test ('stand up, take your mat, and walk').

questions.question: In a synagogue on the Sabbath, religious leaders watch closely to see if Jesus will heal a man's withered hand so they can accuse him. What griefs and angers Jesus before he heals the man?
options: That the man with the withered hand refused to ask for help out loud
That his own disciples were arguing about who should sit in the front row
That the leaders' stubborn loyalty to rule-keeping made them silent when asked if it is right to save life
That the synagogue ruler locked the doors to keep the poor outside
questions.explanation: Mark 3:4-5 shows bureaucratic hardness at its worst: when an institution cares more about catching a technical violation than relieving human suffering right in front of it, its moral compass is dead.

questions.question: When a violent squall swamps their boat on the Sea of Galilee while Jesus sleeps on a cushion in the stern, what accusation do the panicked disciples shout to wake him?
options: 'Why did you command us to sail without checking the weather?'
'Don't you care if we drown?'
'Wake up and help us bail the water before the hull cracks!'
'Tell Peter to turn the rudder back toward Capernaum!'
questions.explanation: Under acute panic, human psychology immediately equates silence or stillness with indifference ('Don't you care?'), mistaking calm authority for neglect.

questions.question: After Jesus restores a violent, tormented man who lived in the tombs of the Gerasenes—and a herd of two thousand pigs drowns in the lake—how do the local townspeople react?
options: They throw a feast to celebrate that their dangerous neighbor is finally sane and clothed
They bring every sick person in the region and ask Jesus to stay as their governor
They are seized with fear and beg Jesus to leave their territory because of the economic disruption
They arrest the herdsmen for failing to guard the livestock on the hillside
questions.explanation: Mark 5:15-17 exposes a chilling real-world calculation: the town preferred living next to a familiar human tragedy in the graveyard over dealing with a disruptive healer who upset their livestock economy.

questions.question: King Herod actually respects John the Baptist and protects him in prison. Why does Herod ultimately give the order to have John beheaded anyway?
options: He discovers a secret letter proving John is plotting a military coup with Rome's enemies
He makes a reckless public oath at a banquet and is too afraid of losing face in front of his dinner guests to back down
The Roman emperor threatens to strip Herod of his tetrarchy unless John is executed
John refuses to perform a miracle for Herod's visiting generals
questions.explanation: Mark 6:26 is a textbook study in cowardice disguised as power: Herod was deeply distressed, yet he murdered an innocent man because he was more terrified of looking weak in front of his banquet guests.

questions.question: In Mark 8, Jesus poses a famous cost-benefit question about human ambition: what is the fatal flaw in a strategy that gains the entire world?
options: The tax burden of maintaining a global empire eventually bankrupts the treasury
You can win every external prize on earth while forfeiting your own soul in the process
Your rivals will inevitably assassinate you before you can enjoy the wealth
No single ruler can master all the languages required to govern the nations
questions.explanation: Jesus frames the ultimate bad trade in plain economic terms: winning the whole board while losing yourself is a net-zero bankruptcy.

questions.question: A desperate father brings his convulsing son to Jesus after the disciples fail to help. When Jesus says all things are possible for one who believes, what raw, honest answer does the father cry out?
options: 'I have never doubted for a single moment since my son was born!'
'I believe; help my unbelief!'
'Punish your disciples first for wasting my time at the bottom of the mountain!'
'Show me a sign in the sky so I can be certain before I trust you!'
questions.explanation: Mark 9:24 shows that real trust isn't pretending you have 100% certainty—Jesus honors the father who admits his faith and his doubt are happening at the exact same time.

questions.question: A wealthy, morally disciplined man runs up to Jesus asking what he lacks for eternal life, having kept the commandments since youth. Why does he walk away grieving when Jesus tells him to sell his holdings and give to the poor?
options: Because he had already pledged his estate to the Jerusalem temple treasury
Because his wealth wasn't just an asset he owned—it was the functional security he refused to trade away
Because Roman law prohibited citizens from liquidating ancestral land
Because Jesus refused to let him say goodbye to his family first
questions.explanation: Mark 10:21 says Jesus looked at him and loved him before naming the one thing holding him hostage: his moral record was clean, but his net worth was his actual god.

questions.question: Right after Jesus explains for the third time that he is heading to Jerusalem to be mocked and executed, what do James and John privately pull him aside to ask?
options: For permission to return to Galilee to protect their aging father Zebedee
For the top two executive seats at his right and left hand when he takes power
For a private explanation of why Judas is carrying the group's money bag
For weapons to defend him when the temple guards arrive
questions.explanation: While Jesus is talking about sacrifice, his inner circle is lobbying for corner-office promotions—prompting Jesus to redefine leadership as service rather than lording rank over others.

questions.question: Watching donors drop money into the temple treasury, why does Jesus say a poor widow who dropped in two tiny copper coins contributed more than all the wealthy donors combined?
options: Because her coins were antique silver pieces worth more than their face value
Because the wealthy gave out of their surplus buffer, while she gave 100% of what she had to live on
Because the wealthy donors were using counterfeit Roman currency
Because she was the only person who prayed aloud while dropping the coins
questions.explanation: Jesus measures generosity not by the size of the check, but by how much skin is in the game—what remains in your pocket after you give.

questions.question: When Jesus speaks in his hometown synagogue in Nazareth, the crowd initially praises him—until he reminds them that Elijah and Elisha helped foreign outsiders rather than Israelites. How does his hometown react?
options: They take up an offering to send missionaries to Syria and Sidon
They erupt in rage, drive him out of town, and try to throw him off the cliff
They politely ask him to verify his scroll citations with the elders
They invite the Roman garrison commander to hear the rest of the sermon
questions.explanation: People love a hometown hero as long as he validates their group privilege; the moment Jesus challenges their tribal entitlement, admiration flips into murderous rage in seconds.

questions.question: Simon the Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner but skips every basic courtesy, while a woman known as a sinner washes Jesus' feet with her tears. How does Jesus explain the massive contrast between the two?
options: People who think they have needed very little forgiveness show very little love
Public sinners are naturally more emotional than educated religious scholars
Simon was distracted by managing his household servants during the banquet
The woman was trying to buy social standing among the Pharisee's guests
questions.explanation: In Luke 7:47, Jesus links gratitude directly to self-awareness: Simon's moral superiority made him cold and stingy, while the woman who knew the weight of her debt poured out extravagant gratitude.

questions.question: A legal expert asks Jesus 'Who is my neighbor?' hoping to draw a technical boundary around who he is obligated to care for. How does Jesus flip the question in the parable of the Good Samaritan?
options: He provides a strict geographical radius of five miles around a person's home
He shifts the question from 'Who qualifies for my help?' to 'Whose neighbor am I willing to be?'
He rules that only people who share your religious covenant count as neighbors
He instructs the lawyer to let temple officials handle roadside emergencies
questions.explanation: By making a despised Samaritan the hero who stops, pays the bill, and crosses ethnic lines while religious professionals cross the street, Jesus destroys the lawyer's loophole.

questions.question: While hosting Jesus, Martha gets overwhelmed by all the kitchen prep and demands that Jesus order her sister Mary to get up and help. What does Jesus point out to Martha?
options: That Mary had already finished her share of the cooking earlier that morning
That Martha's frantic, resentful busywork has distracted her from the actual person she is hosting
That guests only need bread and water rather than an elaborate banquet
That the disciples should be the ones serving the meal instead of the sisters
questions.explanation: Luke 10:40-42 highlights a classic burnout trap: turning good hospitality into anxious, score-keeping busyness that resents anyone who slows down to actually be present.

questions.question: In the parable of the rich fool, a landowner has a record harvest, tears down his barns to build bigger ones, and tells himself to relax and enjoy decades of comfort. Why does God call him a fool?
options: Because he built his new barns on an unstable flood plain
Because he hoarded for a guaranteed future while forgetting his life could end that very night
Because he failed to diversify his crops beyond grain and wine
Because he hired dishonest contractors who overcharged him for the timber
questions.explanation: The man treated wealth as permanent insurance against mortality, speaking only to himself ('my grain, my barns, my soul') right up until the night his time ran out.

questions.question: In the parable of the Prodigal Son, after the reckless younger brother comes home broke and is welcomed with a feast, what reveals that the dutiful older brother was just as estranged from the father's heart?
options: He demands the remaining half of the estate in cash and moves to a neighboring town
He refuses to enter the party and bitterly complains that his years of slaving never earned him even a young goat
He hires local guards to arrest his younger brother for squandering family property
He secretly burns the fattened calf in the kitchen before it can be served
questions.explanation: In Luke 15:28-30, the older brother exposes his own transactional motive: he stayed home and followed every rule not out of love for his father, but as a joyless wage-earner keeping score.

questions.question: A Pharisee and a despised tax collector both go to the temple to pray. Why does Jesus say only the tax collector walked home right with God?
options: Because the tax collector donated a larger percentage of his income that afternoon
Because the Pharisee's prayer was just a resume of his superiority over others, while the tax collector owned his need for mercy
Because the Pharisee recited his prayer in the wrong court of the temple
Because the tax collector promised to resign from his Roman post before sunset
questions.explanation: Luke 18:11 literally notes the Pharisee 'prayed with himself'—using prayer to congratulate himself for not being like the guy standing ten feet away.

questions.question: When Jesus bypasses the religious elite in Jericho and invites himself to stay at the house of Zacchaeus—the city's chief tax collector—how does Zacchaeus prove his inner change is real and not just talk?
options: He writes a formal apology letter to the local synagogue elders
He immediately pledges half his wealth to the poor and fourfold restitution to anyone he defrauded
He burns his Roman tax ledgers in the public square
He offers to fund Jesus' travel expenses all the way to Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Real turning points show up in the ledger: without being lectured, Zacchaeus immediately puts his money where his mouth is and makes concrete financial repair.

questions.question: At the Last Supper—mere minutes after Jesus announces that one of them is about to betray him—what argument breaks out among the disciples around the table?
options: Which of them should be reckoned the greatest in rank
Whether they should flee to Bethany or stay inside the city walls
Who should guard the door against the temple police
Why Judas was allowed to dip his bread in the same dish
questions.explanation: Luke 22:24 is a stunning snapshot of human ego: in the middle of the gravest night in history, the twelve immediately pivot from 'Who is the traitor?' to 'Which of us is number one?'

questions.question: Two disillusioned disciples walking to Emmaus explain to a stranger that they had hoped Jesus was the one to redeem Israel before he was crucified. Why had their hope collapsed?
options: They assumed a true Messiah would overthrow Rome immediately rather than suffer first as the prophets described
They heard a rumor that the Roman governor had sealed all the roads out of Judea
They believed the other ten disciples had already surrendered to the high priest
They had never heard the Old Testament prophecies about Moses and the prophets
questions.explanation: Their expectations were built on a selective reading of victory without suffering; Jesus walks them through the whole storyline of Scripture to show why the cross was the mission, not a detour.

questions.question: Nicodemus, a high-ranking Pharisee and member of the Jewish ruling council, seeks out Jesus—but comes at night. What does Jesus immediately challenge in their conversation?
options: Nicodemus's refusal to pay the Roman tribute tax
Nicodemus's assumption that his elite credentials and pedigree are enough without a total spiritual rebirth
Nicodemus's vote in the council to arrest John the Baptist
Nicodemus's lack of knowledge of the Greek language
questions.explanation: Coming under cover of darkness to protect his institutional reputation, Nicodemus expects a polite peer-to-peer debate, but Jesus tells the credentialed insider he has to start over from scratch.

questions.question: At Jacob's well at noon, when Jesus gently reveals that he knows all about the Samaritan woman's five past husbands and current partner, what classic deflection move does she immediately try?
options: She drops her water jar and runs back into town without saying another word
She pivots the conversation to a safe, abstract religious debate about which mountain is the right place to worship
She claims she is actually related to the town magistrate of Sychar
She blames the local elders for refusing to grant her a legal divorce
questions.explanation: In John 4:19-20, the instant a conversation gets uncomfortably personal, she changes the subject to an ancient theological controversy—a textbook human defense mechanism.

questions.question: By the pool of Bethesda, Jesus approaches a man who has been disabled for thirty-eight years and asks a seemingly obvious question: 'Do you want to get well?' How does the man initially respond?
options: He shouts 'Yes!' and tries to crawl toward Jesus
Instead of saying yes, he recites his excuse about why no one ever helps him and others always cut in front of him
He asks Jesus for silver coins rather than physical healing
He tells Jesus that the Sabbath rules forbid him from moving his mat
questions.explanation: After 38 years in the same spot, helplessness and grievance can become an identity; Jesus' sharp question cuts straight past three decades of blaming others to demand agency.

questions.question: The day after Jesus feeds five thousand people with loaves and fish, the crowd tracks him down across the lake. Why does Jesus refuse to be flattered by their enthusiasm?
options: He knows the Roman authorities paid them to spy on his movements
He calls them out directly for chasing him because their stomachs were filled, not because they cared about the truth
He realizes they left the leftover baskets behind on the other shore
He knows they are planning to hand him over to Herod's soldiers
questions.explanation: In John 6:26, Jesus strips away the illusion of crowd popularity: they wanted a free catering service and a political vending machine, and most walked away by the end of the chapter when he refused to play along.

questions.question: Religious leaders drag a woman caught in adultery into the temple courts to trap Jesus between Roman law (which forbade them from executing her) and Moses' law. How does Jesus dismantle the ambush in one sentence?
options: He demands that they produce the man who was with her before proceeding
He tells the crowd that whoever among them is without sin should be the first to throw a stone at her
He appeals the case directly to Pontius Pilate's tribunal
He declares that the law of Moses no longer applies inside the city walls
questions.explanation: Without excusing the offense or breaking the law, Jesus turns the spotlight back onto the mob's own conscience—causing the accusers to drop their stones and walk out from the oldest to the youngest.

questions.question: When a man born blind is healed by Jesus on the Sabbath, the Pharisees interrogate the man, his parents, and the man a second time. Why do they ultimately throw him out of the synagogue?
options: Because he admits he made up the story to collect more alms at the gate
Because the undeniable evidence of his eyesight destroys their ideological premise, and he mocks their refusal to accept the facts
Because he refuses to pay the required temple purification fee
Because his parents testify that he was never actually blind
questions.explanation: John 9 is a masterclass in confirmation bias: when hard reality ('One thing I do know: I was blind but now I see') contradicts an institution's dogma, the institution expels the witness rather than admit error.

questions.question: When Mary of Bethany pours a jar of expensive perfume on Jesus' feet, Judas Iscariot objects loudly that it should have been sold and the money given to the poor. What does John note was Judas's actual motive?
options: He was trying to impress the visiting Jerusalem priests with his frugality
He didn't care about the poor at all—he kept the common money bag and routinely skimmed from what went into it
He owed a personal debt to the merchant who sold Mary the perfume
He was angry that his own gift to Jesus looked small by comparison
questions.explanation: John 12:4-6 highlights how often corrupt self-interest disguises itself in the language of noble social concern.

questions.question: Knowing that the Father had put all things under his power, what does Jesus immediately get up from the supper table and do in John 13?
options: He dictates the organizational hierarchy for the twelve apostles after his departure
He wraps a towel around his waist and washes the dirty feet of his disciples—including Judas and Peter
He marches to the temple courts to confront the high priest Caiaphas
He divides his possessions among his mother and brothers
questions.explanation: Notice the causal link in John 13:3-5: it isn't insecurity that makes someone serve; it is total security in who he is that frees Jesus to take the lowest servant's job in the room.

questions.question: On the morning they bring Jesus to Pontius Pilate to demand his execution, why do the religious accusers refuse to step inside the Roman governor's palace?
options: They are afraid Pilate's bodyguards will arrest them alongside Jesus
They want to avoid ceremonial defilement so they can still eat the Passover meal with a 'clean' conscience
Roman law forbade local citizens from entering the praetorium before sunrise
They are protesting Pilate's recent seizure of temple funds
questions.explanation: John 18:28 exposes the ultimate compartmentalization of conscience: meticulously protecting external ritual purity on the outside while orchestrating a judicial murder on the inside.

questions.question: On the beach in Galilee, right after Jesus restores Peter and tells him the hard road ahead of him, Peter spots John following and asks, 'Lord, what about him?' How does Jesus shut down Peter's comparison?
options: He promises Peter that John will face the exact same trials in Ephesus
He tells Peter that John's storyline is none of his business: 'What is that to you? You must follow me'
He appoints Peter to supervise John's ministry in Jerusalem
He rebukes John for eavesdropping on a private conversation
questions.explanation: Even after forgiveness and commissioning, the human instinct is to look sideways to see if someone else got an easier deal; Jesus tells Peter to keep his eyes in his own lane.

questions.question: When the Sanhedrin arrests Peter and John—two unschooled, ordinary fishermen—and orders them never to speak Jesus' name again, why is the ruling council backed into a corner?
options: The Roman governor sends troops to protect the fishermen
The forty-year-old man who had been crippled since birth is standing right next to them healed, leaving nothing they can deny
Peter threatens to call down fire on the council chamber
The temple treasury guards go on strike in support of the apostles
questions.explanation: In Acts 4:14-20, institutional intimidation hits a wall against undeniable evidence and men who simply reply that they cannot stop speaking about what they have seen with their own eyes.

questions.question: Ananias and Sapphira sell a piece of property and bring part of the money to the apostles. Since Peter explicitly tells them the land and the cash were 100% theirs to keep, what was their actual crime?
options: Failing to donate the mandatory 100% required of all church members
Conspiring to stage a fake display of total sacrifice to buy the same public prestige Barnabas had received
Selling property that legally belonged to the Jerusalem temple
Refusing to pay the Roman property transfer tax
questions.explanation: In Acts 5:4, Peter makes clear there was zero compulsory communism—they could have kept every penny; what was lethal was faking radical generosity to purchase spiritual clout on a discount.

questions.question: When the furious council wants to execute the apostles in Acts 5, the respected Pharisee Gamaliel stands up and talks them down with what pragmatic historical argument?
options: Executing popular teachers during a festival will trigger a Roman military crackdown
If this movement is merely human, it will fizzle out like past rebellions; if it is from God, you cannot stop it and will only find yourselves fighting God
The apostles should be exiled to Galilee where they have no political influence
Jewish law requires a thirty-day cooling-off period before capital sentences
questions.explanation: Gamaliel uses calm historical realism to check institutional panic: fake movements collapse under their own weight, while truth doesn't need—and can't be crushed by—state violence.

questions.question: As the early Jerusalem church grows rapidly, Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution compared to the Hebrew-speaking widows. How do the apostles solve the crisis?
options: They tell the Greek-speaking families to stop complaining and trust the leadership
They shut down the food program entirely so they can focus on preaching
They acknowledge the operational gap and empower seven respected leaders from the neglected group itself to run the distribution
They divide the church into two separate congregations based on language
questions.explanation: Notice in Acts 6:5 that all seven men chosen to run the food distribution carry Greek names—the leaders didn't get defensive; they handed real authority directly to the underserved group.

questions.question: Simon the Sorcerer in Samaria believes, gets baptized, and follows Philip everywhere—until Peter and John arrive and people receive the Spirit. What action exposes that Simon's old mindset hasn't changed?
options: He challenges Peter to a public magic contest in the city square
He pulls out cash and offers to buy the franchise rights to confer the Spirit on anyone he chooses
He steals the travel funds collected for the Jerusalem church
He demands to be named bishop of Samaria ahead of Philip
questions.explanation: Simon viewed spiritual power as a trade secret to monetize and control an audience, prompting Peter's blazing rebuke: 'May your money perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God!'

questions.question: In Damascus, Ananias is told in a vision to walk over to Straight Street and lay hands on Saul of Tarsus—the exact man who arrived in town with arrest warrants to haul believers away in chains. How does Ananias handle the assignment?
options: He flees Damascus immediately, just as Jonah fled toward Tarshish
He voices his legitimate fear and the hard facts about Saul's reputation, then walks into the house and calls him 'Brother Saul'
He sends a servant ahead to verify whether Saul is actually blind or setting a trap
He demands that the Jerusalem apostles come to Damascus first to vouch for Saul
questions.explanation: Acts 9:13-17 shows real courage: Ananias doesn't pretend Saul isn't dangerous—he states his objection plainly, hears the mission, and walks straight into the room to greet his former persecutor as a brother.

questions.question: Right after uniting to win a massive doctrinal victory at the Jerusalem Council, Paul and Barnabas have such a sharp dispute that they split up their partnership. What triggered the clash?
options: A theological disagreement over whether Gentile converts had to keep the Sabbath
A clash over whether to give a second chance to John Mark, who had deserted them under pressure on the previous trip
A dispute over whether to travel north into Asia or west into Greece
A disagreement over how to divide the missionary funds donated by Antioch
questions.explanation: Acts 15:36-40 doesn't airbrush leadership conflict: Paul prioritized mission reliability while Barnabas prioritized restoring a failed teammate—and decades later in 2 Timothy 4:11, Paul admits Mark became invaluable to him.

questions.question: In Philippi, after Paul and Silas are stripped, beaten with rods, and locked in the inner dungeon stocks, an earthquake at midnight flings every cell door open and unfastens every prisoner's chains. What stops the jailer from killing himself?
options: The town magistrates arrive at the gate to pardon him
Every single prisoner stayed inside the dark cell instead of bolting, and Paul shouts from the dark, 'We are all here!'
Silas grabs the sword out of the jailer's hand at the last second
The Roman soldiers outside barricade the courtyard exit
questions.explanation: Under Roman law, a guard forfeited his life if prisoners escaped; by sacrificing their own easy escape to save the life of the man who locked them up, Paul and Silas transform the jailer's entire household.

questions.question: In Athens, Paul is deeply provoked by a city full of idols, yet when he stands before the philosophers of the Areopagus, how does he open his case?
options: He denounces Greek philosophy as demonic and quotes the book of Leviticus
He builds a bridge from their own 'To an Unknown God' altar and quotes their own Greek poets to make his case
He challenges the Stoic and Epicurean leaders to a miracle-working duel
He demands that the city council tear down the Parthenon statues
questions.explanation: Even though Paul was inwardly distressed (Acts 17:16), he didn't lead with outrage—he studied the culture, found a point of contact inside their worldview, and used their own literature to reframe reality.

questions.question: In Ephesus, a violent riot fills the theater with thousands chanting 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for two hours. How did Demetrius the silversmith actually start the riot behind closed doors?
options: By warning his fellow guild craftsmen that Paul's message was hurting their high-margin business selling silver shrines
By discovering that Paul's companions had defaced the temple of Artemis
By receiving a vision from the temple priestesses calling for a holy war
By protesting a new Roman tariff on imported silver ore
questions.explanation: Acts 19:24-27 pulls back the curtain on how public outrage is manufactured: behind the loud religious and patriotic slogans in the street was a trade union protecting its profit margin.
